# Tool Use Principles {.unnumbered}

Part II gave the agent a working set for each call, attention state held at a known cost, and durable evidence checked against its source, but nothing it builds changes the world outside the model. Part III follows the path by which a proposal becomes an effect, a tool call that reads a file, restarts a service, or sends a message, and so builds closure for the authority exposure of H·S·A. Authority covers what an action can read and send as well as what it can change. A read-only tool that returns a customer record into context, or a sandbox with an open network route, can leak data without mutating anything, so read access is exposure too. Two questions decide whether an effect is safe, and the part answers them in order. The first is whether the call may happen at all and, once dispatched, whether it happens exactly once. The second is how far the code behind a permitted call can reach once it runs.

::: {#pri-vol3-strict-action-abi .callout-principle title="The typed action contract"}

**Invariant**: A tool call reaches the environment only as a typed proposal that the runtime validates against a closed schema and authorizes against grants the session explicitly holds. A server that advertises a tool establishes that the tool exists, never that this session may invoke it. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-mcp.

**Implication**: Each tool's schema, side-effect class, and required grant live in a descriptor the runtime owns, not in the protocol that discovered the tool. Grammar-constrained decoding removes parse failures but replaces neither validation nor authorization. Rejected proposals return a structured diagnostic to the model, and observations returning across the boundary are bounded and typed before they enter context.

:::

Validation and authorization decide whether a call may be dispatched. They say nothing about what the runtime should do when the dispatch times out.

::: {#pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement .callout-principle title="Settlement before retry"}

**Invariant**: A timeout on a mutating dispatch carries no information about whether the effect occurred. The request may have been lost, the tool may have crashed partway through the mutation, or the mutation may have committed and only its reply been lost. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency.

**Implication**: The runtime retries a non-idempotent action only under an idempotency key the endpoint deduplicates, or after a read-only probe shows the environment still in its pre-dispatch state. A probe that finds an intermediate state halts autonomous action until recovery, and any execution lease must outlast the timeout it protects.

:::

An authorized, settled call still runs code the model chose, and often code the model wrote.

::: {#pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing .callout-principle title="Containment beneath the model"}

**Invariant**: A model reads system instructions and untrusted data as one sequence of tokens, so no instruction to the model can guarantee that its next proposal is safe. Every dispatched action therefore runs inside an envelope enforced by a layer below the code it contains, and nothing inside that envelope reaches the host, another tenant, or the network except through channels the runtime controls. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-blast-radius.

**Implication**: The strength of the envelope follows from the code it runs, the authority the task holds, and how long it holds it. Arbitrary native code needs its own guest kernel behind hardware virtualization, while pure computation can run in a bytecode sandbox with no direct system calls. Capabilities inside the envelope can only narrow over a trajectory, credentials stay outside it and are attached by the egress proxy, and network egress reaches only named destinations. Envelopes are reset by destruction or snapshot rollback, never by cleaning in place, and their start-up cost is recovered by keeping ready envelopes in a pool rather than by weakening the boundary.

:::

@Sec-vol3-tool-calling builds the first two principles into the tool-call loop: a descriptor for every tool, a per-call grant the runtime decides, a dispatch that settles before it retries, and an observation shaped before it enters context. @Sec-vol3-sandboxes starts where the grant stops. It builds the third principle into capabilities, an isolation envelope, a per-trajectory workspace, and egress and dataflow controls, priced in start-up latency and memory. Both chapters work on one action at a time. A trajectory strings hundreds of such actions across hours, and keeping it bounded, approved, and recoverable over that horizon is the work of Part IV.
